Dear Information Rights / Archives Team,

I am writing to request information under the Freedom of Information Act
2000 (or equivalent records access) regarding my grandfather, Mr. Williams,
who worked in the engineering department of the Cardiff Post Office /
General Post Office around 1897.

Specifically, I seek any records, personnel files, correspondence, reports,
or mentions confirming his involvement in Guglielmo Marconi’s wireless
telegraphy experiments at Lavernock Point (including erecting the 120-foot
pole and related tests to Flat Holm). This relates to contemporary
newspaper reports from May 1897.

Please provide:

   - Any personnel or service records for Mr. Williams in the Cardiff
   engineering department circa 1897.
   - Documents referencing "Mr. Williams" in connection with Marconi’s
   demonstrations.
   - Any other relevant historical files from the GPO telegraph/engineering
   teams.

My full name: Requester Address: █████, Vale of
Glamorgan, █████ Contact: █████ Relationship: Great
Grandson

I am ultimately seeking any record about my great grandfather Mr Williams
of Great House Farm, Llandough, Cardiff (formerly Vale of Glamorgan). Not
to be confused with Great House Farm, Llandough, Cowbridge, Vale of
Glamorgan. And his role in the Marconi experiment. And before and after
Marconis stay with our family in our home in 1897.

I am happy to provide further identification if required. Thank you for
your assistance.

Best regards,

Requester

records.transcript:
*Editor / Investigations Desk*

Dear Editor,

I am writing to ask your investigations team to examine what I believe is a
significant public-interest story involving one of the most influential
adverse possession cases in modern English and Welsh property law: *BP
Properties Ltd v Buckler [1987] 2 EGLR 168* (also reported as *(1988) 55 P
& CR 337*).

This Court of Appeal decision continues to be cited in legal textbooks and
case law. It established that a unilateral letter from the paper title
owner granting a rent-free licence could prevent adverse possession, even
where the occupier had not expressly accepted it. The case has shaped
property law for almost forty years.

My concern is not simply with the legal judgment itself.

It is with what surrounded it.

For several years I have been investigating the history of my family's
occupation of *Great House Farm, Llandough, near Penarth*, and the events
leading to the litigation. Through hundreds of Freedom of Information
requests, archive searches, Land Registry enquiries, historical research
and correspondence with public authorities, I have uncovered what I believe
are serious inconsistencies, missing records and evidence of institutional
concealment that deserve independent scrutiny.

Among the matters that I believe warrant investigation are:

   - Whether material evidence relating to the occupation and ownership of
   Great House Farm was withheld or never presented.
   - The circumstances surrounding the registration of title by BP
   interests in 1982 despite the long-running dispute.
   - Missing or unexplained historical records across multiple public
   bodies.
   - Whether public authorities have failed to preserve records concerning
   a nationally significant legal case.
   - Whether subsequent institutions have frustrated attempts to obtain
   records through Freedom of Information legislation.
   - The wider implications if a leading legal precedent was built upon an
   incomplete or inaccurate factual record.

My investigation has revealed repeated examples of authorities either
claiming records do not exist, directing me elsewhere, or providing
documents unrelated to the requests made. Numerous archives acknowledge
gaps where relevant material would ordinarily be expected.

I have also experienced what I believe to be persistent obstruction. My
elected representatives have failed to engage despite repeated requests.
Complaints have been redirected without investigation. During my enquiries,
a court employee whom I challenged over contradictory information left
their position shortly afterwards. While I cannot infer the reason for that
departure, the wider pattern has made it exceptionally difficult to
establish an accurate historical record.

This story extends far beyond a private family dispute.

It concerns:

   - whether powerful institutions have been properly held accountable;
   - preservation of public records;
   - transparency within government;
   - the development of UK property law;
   - the treatment of ordinary families in litigation against major
   corporations;
   - and whether historical injustices can remain effectively hidden
   because records disappear over time.

The human story is equally compelling.

My family lived through decades of litigation, uncertainty and eventual
displacement. The farmhouse was ultimately demolished, ending centuries of
family association with the property. Much of my family—particularly the
women—have lived with the consequences for generations and remain reluctant
to speak publicly because of the trauma. My brother and I are now
attempting to reconstruct the historical record before more evidence
disappears.

The property itself has remarkable historical significance. Great House
Farm has connections with the historic Bute Estate, archaeological
discoveries including Roman remains, and local accounts associated with the
pioneering wireless experiments at Lavernock Point during the Marconi era.
Yet the legal battle that made national case law has largely eclipsed that
wider history.

This investigation is supported by:

   - extensive documentary evidence;
   - Land Registry correspondence;
   - Freedom of Information responses from multiple public authorities;
   - archive references from national and local repositories;
   - court documents;
   - historical maps;
   - newspaper reports;
   - and a detailed chronology spanning more than a century.

I have also recorded my █████ explaining the evidence, chronology and
impact on my family: https://youtu.be/XuArB_vYWWA?si=O7TL2i5ocU3vn5fG

I am prepared to provide your journalists with a fully indexed evidence
archive, original source documents, timelines, witness information where
available, and copies of all official correspondence.

I am *not* asking your newspaper to accept my conclusions without question.

I am asking you to investigate.

If my concerns are unfounded, they should be capable of being disproved
through proper scrutiny. If they are substantiated, they raise serious
questions about one of the UK's leading property law authorities,
institutional accountability, public record keeping and the treatment of an
ordinary family whose story has never properly been told.

This is not simply a historical dispute.

It is a story about how legal precedents are created, how power operates,
whether the historical record can be trusted, and whether ordinary citizens
can ever obtain accountability decades after the events in question.

I believe it is exactly the kind of investigation that serves the public
interest.

I would welcome the opportunity to speak with one of your investigative
journalists and provide unrestricted access to the evidence I have
assembled.

*Yours faithfully,*

*Requester*
Retired Sergeant, 

█████

Dear Archive Team,

I am conducting historical research into the General Post Office's
involvement in Guglielmo Marconi's wireless demonstrations in South Wales
during 1897.

Post Office Ltd has advised that your archive is the most likely repository
for surviving historic GPO records relating to this period.

I would be grateful if you could search for any records relating to:

   - Great House Farm, Llandough, near Penarth, Cardiff (not Great House
   Farm, Llandough near Cowbridge).
   - Llandough, Penarth, Lavernock and the surrounding wireless
   demonstration sites.
   - Guglielmo Marconi's 1897 demonstrations.
   - GPO Telegraph or Engineering Department records concerning these
   demonstrations.
   - Correspondence, reports, notebooks, diaries, staff lists, expense
   █████, photographs or plans relating to engineers or officials present.
   - Any references to Mr Williams of Great House Farm, Llandough, who
   family history suggests assisted Marconi before, during or after his stay
   at the property.

If records relating specifically to Mr Williams cannot be located, I would
also appreciate details of any records identifying GPO personnel, visitors
or local residents connected with the demonstrations, as these may help
establish the historical context.

If another archive holds any of these records, I would be grateful if you
could advise where I should direct my enquiry.

Mr Williams of Great House Farm was my great grandad. I am trying to
ascertain if the Mr Williams post office worker, mentioned helping Marconi
in the article, was the same man as my great grandfather. I am also looking
for any more connections between my family, my former home and Marconi and
the radio experiments at lavernock point. Which I understand were already
underway before Marconi arrived to South Wales.

Thank you for your time and assistance. I look forward to your response.

Kind regards,

records.transcript:
Dear Freedom of Information Team,

I am writing to request information under the Freedom of Information Act
2000 and, where applicable, the Environmental Information Regulations 2004.

A published local history account states that, during works to replace the
stone floor of the dining room at Great House Farm (also known as Ty Mawr),
Llandough, Cardiff, the remains of a soldier and his horse were discovered
beneath the floor.

 The remains were subsequently re-buried in the churchyard, and the
soldier’s visor and lance were given to the National Museum of Wales
(Amgueddfa Cymru).

I therefore request the following recorded information held by Amgueddfa
Cymru:

Any records relating to the acquisition, accession, donation, transfer or
deposit of a medieval visor, lance, helmet, or other items of armour
associated with Great House Farm / Ty Mawr / Llandough.

The accession number(s), date of acquisition or transfer, name of the donor
or transferring body, and any provenance or discovery notes linked to these
objects.

Any catalogue entries, object records, or internal correspondence
concerning the above items.

Any records of associated human or animal remains from the same discovery,
including notes on reburial.

Any related excavation, watching-brief, or discovery reports held by the
Museum.

If any of the requested information is already publicly available (for
example via the Museum’s online collections database), I would be grateful
if you could simply provide the relevant accession numbers or catalogue
links.

Please treat this as a request for recorded information only. I am not
seeking advice or opinion.

I look forward to your response within the statutory timescale.

Yours faithfully,

Requester

With great regret I am writing to make a complaint about the persistent
failure of Councillor George D. D. Carroll (Llandough ward) to respond
substantively to my repeated and reasonable correspondence concerning
historic land, planning, enforcement, heritage and related public-interest
matters at Great House Farm (Ty Mawr), Llandough (now Church View Close),
Vale of Glamorgan.

I have a legitimate and long-standing family interest in the site
(Williams/Buckler family connection documented from the 17th century). See
attached.

The issues raised include █████ defective notices, loss of opportunity to
contest enforcement leading to demolition in 1988, heritage/regulatory
oversight, planning and title records, and related transparency failures.

Despite multiple contacts over several months, I have received no
substantive replies from Cllr Carroll. This constitutes a failure to
respond and a failure to deal with the case properly.

### Full correspondence log with Cllr George Carroll (
█████)

| Date       | Subject / Key content
                         | Response received |
|------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------|
| 16 Feb 2026 | Potential gaps in Council planning/record-keeping for Great
House Farm (demolished 1988); title █████ and procedural issues relating to
Church View Close | None |

| 4 May 2026  | Request regarding BP vs Buckler 1987; shared
media/evidence; request for attention as Llandough councillor | None |

| 7 Jun 2026  | “Church View Close, Llandough” – piecing together 1988
events from public records, family █████ and media | None |

| 25 Jun 2026 | “Great House Farm, Llandough” – enquiry whether prior
concerns on family dispossession had been reviewed; request for any
progress or discussion | None |

| 13 Jul 2026 | “Great House Farm/ Church View Close” – formal follow-up
listing the above timeline, restating legitimate interest (family roots
since 1667), noting absence of replies, requesting detailed response within
10 working days, and raising the removed commemorative tree | None |

### Remedy sought

1. A full written response from Cllr Carroll addressing the points raised
in the logged emails, within 10–15 working days.

2. Confirmation that this complaint has been logged under the Council’s
corporate complaints procedure and/or referred to the Monitoring Officer /
Standards Committee as appropriate for any potential breach of the
councillor Code of Conduct (failure to respond / failure to deal properly
with a case).

3. Written confirmation of the process and timescale for investigation and
response.

I have retained the full original emails and attachments and can supply
them on request. Please acknowledge receipt of this formal complaint.

Yours sincerely,

Requester

Ms Longford,

Thank you for your email.

I note your confirmation that Cadw holds no transfer lists, accession
records, archive schedules or other documentation recording whether records
relating to Great House Farm were transferred to the RCAHMW, and that Cadw
also holds no record of their destruction. I also note that the suggestion
that records may have been transferred or destroyed is based upon an
inspector's understanding of historic practice rather than documentary
evidence relating to this case.

However, there remain a small number of points on which I would be grateful
for clarification.

   1.

   The original response of 11 June stated that associated records "would
   have been either transferred to the RCAHMW or destroyed under the Public
   Records Act 1958". As no transfer or destruction documentation has been
   identified, on what evidential basis was that statement made?
   2.

   Does the Welsh Government now accept that it holds no documentary
   evidence that any records relating to Great House Farm were transferred to
   the RCAHMW?
   3.

   Contemporary press reports concerning the proposed protection of Great
   House Farm referred to consultation with other departments and bodies
   before a decision was reached. During this correspondence I therefore asked
   whether searches extended to correspondence with other departments,
   external bodies and related records. Although you have confirmed wider
   searches were undertaken, no such records have been identified. Could you
   therefore confirm whether the Welsh Government's position is that it holds
   no surviving correspondence, memoranda, consultation records or other
   documents relating to any such consultations concerning Great House Farm?
   4.

   Is the Welsh Government's position therefore that, apart from the two
   photographs dated 29 July 1988, no inspection report, recommendation,
   consultation correspondence, assessment, case file or associated
   documentation relating to the 1988 consideration of Great House Farm
   survives?

These questions are intended solely to clarify the historical record and to
reconcile the original response with the findings of the internal review.

Thank you for your assistance, and I look forward to your reply.

Yours sincerely,

Requester

>
> Thank you for your letter of 2 July 2026 responding to the internal review
> of my Freedom of Information request (ATISN 27021) concerning Great House

>
> I appreciate the additional searches undertaken during the review and the
> explanation provided regarding the physical record series examined.
>

> the outcome of the internal review, I would be be grateful if you could
> clarify a number of points which appear to remain unresolved.
>

>
> The original response stated that Great House Farm was visited and
> assessed by Cadw inspectors and that the building did not satisfy the
> statutory listing criteria.
>
> The internal review now confirms that no assessment, report or case file
> relating to that decision has been located and further states that any
> relevant file may have been destroyed before being entered onto the
> electronic records system.
>
> Please therefore identify the documentary basis upon which the original
> response concluded that the property was assessed and found not to meet the
> listing criteria.
>
> Specifically:
>
>    - Is that conclusion derived from a surviving record?
>    - If so, please identify that record.
>    - If not, please explain how that conclusion was reached.
>
> *2. The inspection of 29 July 1988*
>
> The original disclosure included two photographs dated 29 July 1988.
>
> Please confirm:
>
>    - whether those photographs were taken as part of a formal listing
>    inspection;
>    - whether they formed part of a wider inspection file;
>    - whether any inspection notes, recommendation forms, field notebooks,
>    photographic registers or other associated records were created; and
>    - if such records once existed, whether they are now believed to have
>    been destroyed.
>
> *3. Basis for the statement that records may have been destroyed*
>
> The review states that it is possible documentation dating from around
> 1988 was destroyed before being entered onto the electronic records system.
>
> Please clarify whether that statement is based upon:
>
>    - documentary evidence relating specifically to Great House Farm;
>    - records management documentation such as retention schedules,
>    destruction registers or disposal logs; or
>    - a general understanding of historic records management practices.
>
> If no destruction records exist for the relevant file series, please
> confirm this.
>
> *4. Scope of the searches*
>
> Please confirm whether searches extended beyond the registered listing
> files to include, where appropriate:
>
>    - ministerial correspondence;
>    - senior officials' correspondence;
>    - legal files;
>    - inspector's working papers;
>    - site visit records;
>    - archaeological or conservation files;
>    - policy records; and
>    - correspondence with external organisations, including the Vale of
>    Glamorgan Council, the former Welsh Office and other heritage bodies.
>
> If any of these categories were not searched, I would be grateful if you
> could identify which.
>
> *5. Welsh Government's position*
>
> Finally, I would be appreciate clarification of the Welsh Government's
> position regarding Great House Farm.
>
> Does the Welsh Government's position now amount to one of the following:
>
>    - that Great House Farm was never considered for statutory protection;
>    - that it was considered, but the records no longer survive; or
>    - that it is no longer possible to determine whether consideration
>    took place because the relevant records are unavailable?
>

> you could explain what the Welsh Government's position is.
>
> These questions arise directly from the original response and the internal
> review and are intended to clarify the historical record rather than seek
> the creation of new information.

Dear Mathilde,

Thank you very much for taking the time to carry out these searches and for
your detailed response.

I appreciate the clarification regarding the distinction between Great
House Farm, Llandough near Penarth and the similarly named location near
Cowbridge. The Penarth/Llandough/Lavernock area is the location of interest.

Your advice regarding BT Archives is very helpful, and I will follow this
up with them, as the surviving GPO Telegraph and wireless records appear
likely to be held there.

I am also grateful for the information about the Post Office family history
records. My main interest is not that Mr Williams was necessarily a Post
Office employee, but whether the individual mentioned in contemporary
accounts as assisting Marconi at Great House Farm can be identified. Family
history passed down through my great grandfather's line suggests that a Mr
Williams of Great House Farm assisted Marconi during his South Wales
experiments, and I am trying to establish whether this can be connected to
my ancestor.

If possible, could you let me know whether the search you carried out
included any of the following terms or collections, as this may help me
understand the scope of the search:

   - Great House Farm (Llandough/Penarth)
   - Llandough
   - Lavernock
   - Marconi
   - wireless telegraphy demonstrations (1897)
   - GPO Telegraph Department / Engineering Department

I will also contact Glamorgan Archives, as you suggest, since local
newspapers, estate records, or correspondence may contain information not
held in the national collections.

Thank you again for your assistance. Your guidance has helped narrow down
where the relevant evidence is most likely to survive.

Kind regards,

Requester
